Reported Speech
You use reported speech when you are saying (reporting) what other people said.
When reporting speech about events in the past, you usually need to change the verb to a past form that expresses a more distant past.

For example:
Direct speech
  • I am more prepared now.

Reported speech
  • He said he was more prepared now.

When changing sentences from direct speech, check if you have to change the following:
  • pronouns (I said → He said)
  • Present tense verbs
  • Place and time expressions
  • Tenses (backshift → change to the past)
Some reporting verbs and expressions commonly used are: say, tell, and ask.
Other reporting verbs you can use are: comment, suggest, observe, remark, claim. All these verbs follow the pattern: subject + verb (ed) + that + clause.
He told me I needed to work on my interview skills.
He suggested doing a few mock interviews.
He recommended that I practiced with a friend.
He told me that the more I practiced, the better I would get.
My friend Mark said that I should start applying for more jobs.
He mentioned that a few companies were recruiting at the moment.
He said we would put in a good word for me.
Speculating About The Past
When you want to talk about situations in the past in a hypothetical context (not real or necessarily true), you can use the structures would have, should have and could have.
a. The structure could have (+ past participle) describes a situation in which something was possible or that someone had the ability to do something, but they didn't do it.

I could've taken my time.
(= I had the chance to take my time but I didn't)

b. The structure should have (+ past participle) expresses the idea that something is a good idea, but it wasn't done. It is used to express regret or to make a personal judgement about a past action.

You should've texted me!
(= You didn't text me but it was a good idea to do so.)
I know I could've asked for your support.
I don't mean to sound jealous but I could've helped you too.
You could've done this ages ago.
I guess I should've told you your interview skills were not up to snuff.

images.text:
Kristi: Adam, you're late. You should've texted me! I could've taken my time.
Adam: Sorry, Kristi. I got tied up at the fair and then met a friend for coffee. He was helping me ace my next interview. He said I was more prepared now.
Kristi: Oh yeah? What else did he say?
Adam: He told me I needed to work on my interview skills. He suggested doing a few mock interviews.
Kristi: You could've done this ages ago. I guess I should've told you your interview skills were not up to snuff. I'm sorry.
Adam: All good, Kristi. He recommended that I practiced with a friend. Would you mind helping me?
Kristi: Absolutely.

Adam: So, any feedback?
Kristi: Wow. I am impressed. You don't sound overconfident at all. You don't beat around the bush anymore and your answers are on point.
Adam: Thanks. He told me that the more I practiced, the better I would get. I should've followed both your advice from the beginning.
Kristi: You didn't know. It's fine. Have you applied for any jobs?
Adam: My friend Mark said that I should start applying for more jobs. He mentioned that a few companies were recruiting at the moment. He said he would put in a good word for me.

Kristi: That's amazing! I don't mean to sound jealous but I could've helped you too, you know.
Adam: I know I could've asked for your support, but we're both competing for jobs. And you are definitely a stronger candidate.
Kristi: Not anymore. You stand as good a chance as anyone now. So, how do you feel now?
Adam: I feel I've reached a sweet spot. I'm confident in my abilities but still modest enough to know that I still have a lot to learn.
Kristi: Now you can do this with one hand tied behind your back.
